title: Credit Cards
description: Read the statement, keep the grace period, and treat the minimum as a warning.
wolfLine: The minimum is a trap with a due date.

statement-balance.definition: The total you owed on a card at the end of the billing period. Pay this by the due date and you usually avoid interest.
statement-balance.example: A statement balance of $480, paid in full by the due date, means $0 interest on those purchases.

grace-period.definition: The time between the statement date and the due date. Pay the statement balance in full by the due date and new purchases from that period are not charged interest.
grace-period.example: Statement balance $480, due on the 21st. Pay $480 by the 21st and the grace period holds.

cash-advance.definition: Cash you take from a credit card. A fee applies, interest usually starts the same day, and there is no grace period.
cash-advance.example: Take $200 cash. A 5% fee adds $10, so you owe $210 before a single day’s interest.

lessons.title: The Card Statement
lessons.summary: Read a real month on a card: what you spent, what you owe, what’s due.

steps.context: The [[statement balance]] is what you owed when the bill was cut. The [[minimum payment]] is the smallest amount that keeps the account in good standing. The [[due date]] is the last day to pay on time.

lessons.title: The Grace Period
lessons.summary: Pay the statement in full and the interest waits. Carry a balance and it does not.

steps.context: A [[grace period]] is the time between the statement and the [[due date]]. Pay the [[statement balance]] in full by that date and those purchases are not charged interest. Carry a balance, and the grace period usually disappears until you catch up.
steps.prompt: What is a grace period on a credit card?
choices: The stretch after the statement when you can pay in full and skip interest
steps.explain: It is time, not a discount on the price.

steps.prompt: Pay the statement balance by the due date and those purchases usually cost no interest.
steps.explain: That is the grace period doing its job.

steps.prompt: You pay $25 of a $480 statement and leave $455. What happens to the grace period?
choices: It is gone until you pay in full again
It stays, because you paid something
steps.explain: A partial payment is not “in full.”

steps.prompt: Statement balance $640. You pay $640 on the due date. How much interest do you owe on that statement?
steps.explain: Paid in full, on time: $0.

steps.prompt: You lost the grace period last month. A new $50 purchase today is charged interest…
choices: Starting right away, not after a fresh grace period
Only if the purchase is over $500
steps.explain: Until you pay the statement in full, new charges often start accruing immediately.

steps.prompt: Pay the statement balance by the due date and you keep the ___ period.
steps.explain: Grace period.

lessons.title: In Full or the Minimum
lessons.summary: The minimum keeps the account current. The rest keeps costing you.

steps.context: At 24% [[APR]], a rough monthly rate is 2%. Interest lands on what you did not pay.
steps.prompt: Statement balance $625. Minimum $25. You pay the minimum. How much is still unpaid?
About how much interest hits that $600 in the next month?
Of the $25 minimum, if $12 was interest, how much actually cut the balance?
steps.explain: $25 − $12 = $13. Just under half the payment was interest.

steps.prompt: You pay the $625 in full instead. How much interest do you owe on it?
steps.explain: Paid in full: $0, against about $12 if you had paid only the minimum.

steps.prompt: Which payment costs less interest?
steps.explain: Zero interest beats $12, and the $12 repeats.

steps.prompt: The minimum payment is designed to clear a typical card balance in one month.
steps.explain: It is the smallest on-time payment, not a payoff plan.

lessons.title: Nico’s Minimum Trap
lessons.summary: Small payments stretch a balance for years.

story.title: The $50 that barely moved
story.body:
Nico put a **$2,400** TV and sound system on a card that charges **18%** a year, which works out to **1.5%** a month.

The card only asks for a **$50** minimum payment, so that’s what he pays. A friend told him the balance would be gone in about four years. It won’t be.

steps.context: When you pay only the [[minimum payment]], interest takes its share first. Whatever is left is all that touches the [[balance]].
steps.prompt: How much interest does the first month add? (1.5% of $2,400)
He pays the $50 minimum. How much of it cuts the principal?
What is the balance after that one payment?
steps.explain: $2,400 − $14 = $2,386. Next month’s interest is worked out on almost the same debt.

steps.prompt: With no interest at all, how many $50 payments would clear $2,400?
steps.explain: $2,400 ÷ $50 = 48 months: the four years his friend meant. With 1.5% a month of interest, it takes about 86 payments, over seven years.

steps.prompt: What is the trap?
choices: He pays every month and the balance barely moves
The card stops charging interest once he pays the minimum
The minimum rises to cover the interest
steps.explain: Most of each payment is interest.

steps.prompt: Paying more than the minimum, and aiming it at this card, shortens the trap.
steps.explain: Extra dollars go to principal, which cuts next month’s interest.

steps.prompt: Nico can afford $150 this month, not just $50. Where should the extra $100 go?
choices: Into a second purchase on the same card
Into savings while he keeps paying the minimum
steps.explain: At 18%, paying the card down beats almost any savings rate.

lessons.title: Limit and Utilization
lessons.summary: The limit is a ceiling. Using all of it is not the goal.

steps.context: Your [[credit limit]] is the most you can owe on the card. [[Credit utilization]] is the balance divided by that limit. Lower is easier on a [[credit score]].
steps.prompt: Limit $2,000. Balance $500. What is your utilization?
You spend another $700. What is the new balance?
What is utilization on the $2,000 limit now?
The card company raises your limit from $2,000 to $4,000 and you still owe $1,200. What happens to utilization?
steps.explain: $1,200 ÷ $4,000 = 30%. A higher limit helps only if you do not spend it.

steps.prompt: A higher limit is a reason to spend more.
steps.explain: It is room, not a target.

steps.prompt: Which habit keeps utilization in better shape?
choices: Pay the balance down before the statement is cut, when you can
Wait until the card is maxed
steps.explain: The balance that gets reported is the one the score sees.

lessons.title: Cash Advances
lessons.summary: The ATM on your card is the expensive door.

steps.context: A [[cash advance]] is cash you take on a credit card. Expect a fee, often about 5%, and interest that starts immediately. There is no [[grace period]].
steps.prompt: What is a cash advance?
choices: Cash borrowed from the card, usually with a fee and interest from day one
steps.explain: It is a loan inside the card, on worse terms.

steps.prompt: You take a $200 cash advance with a 5% fee. How much is the fee?
What do you owe before any interest?
The cash-advance APR is 30%, about 2.5% a month. Rough interest on $210 for one month?
steps.explain: $210 × 0.025 = $5.25. And it started the day you took the cash.

steps.prompt: A cash advance gets the same grace period as a normal purchase.
steps.explain: Interest starts right away.

steps.prompt: You need $200 before payday. Which is usually cheaper?
choices: Wait, cut a cost, or ask the biller for a few extra days
A second cash advance to pay the fee on the first
steps.explain: The fee plus immediate interest is a steep price for two weeks of cash.

lessons.title: Picking a First Card
lessons.summary: If you pay in full, the fee matters more than the rate.

steps.context: A first card should be one you can pay in full. Compare the annual fee and the [[APR]], and ignore rewards until those two are boring and cheap.

lessons.title: Paying Late
lessons.summary: A late card bill costs a fee, interest, and a mark.

steps.context: Miss a card’s [[due date]] and you can owe a [[late fee]], lose the [[grace period]], and, if it goes 30 days past due, pick up a mark on your [[credit report]].
steps.prompt: You miss the due date. What can the issuer add?
steps.explain: A [[late fee]] is the first hit.

steps.prompt: The bill is $84 and the late fee is $25. What do you owe before any extra interest?
A payment one day late can cost a late fee even if you pay the rest in full.
steps.explain: The due date is a cliff, not a suggestion.

steps.prompt: When does a late card payment become a long-lived credit-report mark?
choices: Once it is about 30 days past due
One hour past the due date
Never, if you pay the late fee
steps.explain: The fee can hit immediately. The seven-year mark is the 30-day version.

steps.prompt: You pay the $84 two days late and the fee is $25. How much extra did being late cost, before interest?
steps.explain: The fee is $25. The $84 was already yours to pay.

steps.prompt: What prevents the fee?
choices: Pay at least the minimum by the due date
Call after the fee posts and hope
steps.explain: On time beats an apology. Autopay the minimum, then pay the rest.
